own_list: Prefix-matched redirect URIs can send authorization codes to an attacker-controlled location.
If the mobile flow lacks PKCE, an intercepted authorization code can be exchanged by another app.
A compromised or malicious partner can redeem points because every partner receives every scope.
A support-console token may be accepted by the rewards API because audience and client restrictions are not checked.
Anyone who obtains bearer tokens from the request logs can replay them to the rewards API.
A stolen mobile refresh token can sustain access indefinitely by repeatedly extending its expiry.
Closed accounts retain refresh tokens that may still mint access tokens unless account status is checked on refresh.
A disconnected partner retains access for the remaining lifetime of its already-issued one-hour access tokens.
A stolen authorization-server session can remain usable during thirty days of inactivity because no idle timeout is defined.
A stolen redeem-scoped token can cash out points without fresh member authentication or transaction approval.
Client-only ledger records cannot establish which member approved a disputed redemption.
MODEL: The rewards API is described as checking only signatures, but the source does not say expiration or all other JWT checks are absent.
14-loyalty-oauth-platform.notes:
Confirming sitting on the rulings applied in #1439, sent as CSV in conversation. The own list is the one written on 2026-10-03 before the recorded sets were opened, carried forward. Changed and new findings were marked afresh; unchanged findings (same fingerprint and same text) carry the reader's 2026-10-03 mark, each reviewed in this ballot. The round 2 missing threats are now claims, so the missing list is empty. n refers to the row number of this ballot, which numbered both cases together.
MODEL: The rewards API model says it checks only signatures. The source says it checks signatures and omits client/audience checks; it does not say expiration or all other JWT checks are absent. Do not propagate rewards API validation behavior to the support console.
Row 19 combines two attack mechanisms under one fingerprint. Preserve the supplied fingerprint for this ballot, then split the claim data and correct the identity rule. Detailed conditional rewrites and the mixed judgment are in its note.
No additional unmatched threat from my own list: its items 1-11 map respectively to ballot rows 1/22, 3/19, 6/30, 9, 18/26, 4/19, 16/31, 32, 15, 17, and 25. Coverage here includes rows requiring correction; it is not a statement that all claims are accepted.
Correction to my own-list items 6 and 9: unlimited sliding lifetime does not alone prove indefinite replay of a copied refresh token; effective sender binding or replay defenses may prevent it. No decided idle timeout is a policy/evidence gap, not proof the deployed server lacks one. Apply the rewrites in 19 and 15.
Row review notes and proposed corrections:
n=1 [asvs V9.2.3 (self-contained-tokens); agree; new]: Supported as an unresolved support-console audience check, not proof the console accepts rewards tokens.
n=2 [asvs V7.3.1 (session-management); agree; changed]: Supported as an undefined timeout policy and unresolved enforcement setting; it no longer asserts that the deployed server has no idle timeout.
n=3 [asvs V7.4.2 (session-management); agree; changed]: Supported as an unresolved account-status check during refresh. Stored token records alone do not establish continued usability.
n=4 [stride spoofing; agree; changed]: The revised conditions correctly separate unlimited sliding lifetime from the unknown defenses against use of a copied token. This is distinct from the authorization-code mechanism in 5.
n=5 [stride spoofing; agree; new]: Supported conditional code-interception threat, now separate from 4. Rationale correction: absence of a client secret does not establish that the code is the only validation input; say server PKCE enforcement is unspecified and the attack depends on acceptance of the intercepted code.
n=6 [stride spoofing; agree; changed]: Supported as a conditional password-guessing scenario, not a demonstrated control failure. Success still requires guessing a valid password; do not infer password weakness from the absence of described defenses.
n=7 [stride tampering; agree; changed]: Supported conditional key-substitution threat. Attacker control of the downloaded key and failure of trusted-source/delivery verification are explicit prerequisites.
n=8 [stride information-disclosure; agree; changed]: Supported conditional exposure of a readable database copy. Reusable refresh-token storage is explicitly conditional, and password hashes are not described as plaintext passwords.
n=9 [stride denial-of-service; agree; changed]: The revised claim explicitly requires exhaustion of capacity despite abuse defenses and correctly limits the immediate effect to obtaining new tokens.
n=10 [stride elevation-of-privilege; agree; changed]: Supported conditional console attack. Both token-audience separation and account-closing authorization must fail; neither failure is established by the shared key or hostname.
n=11 [stride elevation-of-privilege; agree; changed]: The revised claim correctly distinguishes refresh from redemption and makes continued use conditional on both services accepting the closed account. Redemption also remains subject to the existing redeem-scope requirement.
n=26 [asvs V10.4.1 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Prefix matching is explicit. This is the same redirect weakness expressed as an attack in row 42; retain both framework records.
n=27 [asvs V10.4.3 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Ten minutes is explicit and exceeds the one-minute L3 maximum in V10.4.3.
n=28 [asvs V10.4.6 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Supported as an unresolved PKCE requirement, not proof PKCE is absent. Inspect server enforcement as well as the mobile request.
n=29 [asvs V10.4.8 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: The source explicitly gives sliding expiry without an absolute lifetime. Replay resistance is a separate question in row 30.
n=30 [asvs V10.4.5 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Supported as missing evidence about refresh-token replay defenses. At L3, do not treat rotation alone as sufficient; verify sender constraint.
n=31 [asvs V10.4.11 (oauth-and-oidc); duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 46. Keep both under separate-framework scoring; this row records the V10.4.11 scope-assignment requirement. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=32 [asvs V10.2.3 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: The requested scopes are unspecified even though assigned scopes are excessive. This concerns externally operated partner clients; treat it as partner evidence to obtain, not a proven defect in platform-owned code. Authorization requests are not represented by the named token-request flow.
n=33 [asvs V10.4.16 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Shared-secret authentication is explicit and does not meet the stated L3 public-key authentication requirement. Sending the secret in an HTTPS body is not itself evidence of leakage.
n=34 [asvs V10.3.1 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: The rewards API explicitly omits audience checking. A token intended for the support console may therefore be accepted by the rewards API; the reverse direction is not established.
n=35 [asvs V10.3.5 (oauth-and-oidc); agree; unchanged]: Plain bearer tokens are explicit. Missing sender constraint is a separate control gap from the specific log leak in row 45.
n=36 [asvs V10.4.14 (oauth-and-oidc); duplicate; unchanged]: Same underlying sender-constraint finding as 35. Keep both: V10.4.14 addresses authorization-server issuance and V10.3.5 addresses resource-server enforcement, with separate requirement identities. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=37 [asvs V9.2.4 (self-contained-tokens); agree; unchanged]: Supported as an evidence gap: audience inclusion in issued tokens is unspecified. Token issuance and recipient validation are different controls, so this is not a duplicate of 34.
n=38 [asvs V9.1.3 (self-contained-tokens); agree; unchanged]: Supported as an unresolved trust configuration for the downloaded verification key, not evidence that an attacker can replace it.
n=39 [asvs V7.5.3 (session-management); agree; unchanged]: The source expressly says redemption requires only a valid redeem-scoped token, supporting the absence of further transaction authentication or approval.
n=40 [asvs V16.2.5 (security-logging-and-error-handling); duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 45. Keep both under separate-framework scoring; retain V16.2.5 on this ASVS record. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=41 [stride spoofing; agree; unchanged]: Supported conditional credential-compromise scenario: possession of the client secret permits client impersonation. It does not alone grant a member token; retain the need for a valid authorization grant and do not imply the request body leaks the secret.
n=42 [stride information-disclosure; duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 26. Keep both under separate-framework scoring. The attacker must control an accepted prefix-matching URL; code theft alone does not establish redemption without the confidential client secret.
n=43 [stride tampering; agree; unchanged]: A supported conditional threat on the stated ledger-write path. Keep both prerequisites: attacker reachability to the ledger and missing effective authorization/authentication for writes; a cloud foothold alone does not establish either.
n=44 [stride repudiation; agree; unchanged]: The ledger explicitly records the client, not the approving member. Keep the conclusion limited to what that ledger can establish about a particular redemption.
n=45 [stride information-disclosure; agree; unchanged]: Headers are logged and tokens are bearer credentials. Reading a still-valid logged token enables replay within that token's existing permissions and remaining lifetime.
n=46 [stride elevation-of-privilege; agree; unchanged]: Every partner receives every scope, including redemption, although some partners only need balance reads. Member consent to the scopes does not make that excess privilege necessary.
n=47 [stride elevation-of-privilege; agree; unchanged]: Explicit residual-access window after disconnect. Limit impact to the existing token's privileges and remaining lifetime, at most one hour; this is not indefinite access.

own_list: An unauthenticated visitor can enumerate sequential payment-page links to read other companies' invoices and bank details.
A user may open another company's invoice by number if the app fails to enforce ownership on that request.
A viewer may invoke hidden admin actions directly if the server does not enforce roles.
A crafted invoice update can change protected fields such as the paid flag or payout bank account.
Cross-company PDF requests may place another tenant's invoice under the requesting company if the renderer trusts an unchecked job company ID.
A user can flood the single-job PDF renderer with unlimited requests and delay every tenant's PDFs.
A support agent can make changes attributed only to the impersonated customer, concealing the responsible agent.
A stolen customer password is sufficient to take over an account, including an admin account, because there is no second factor.
An omitted company filter can expose other tenants' records because the shared database account has no row-level isolation.
Unspecified internal transport protection leaves interception or alteration of invoice data and render jobs unresolved.
Unspecified encryption at rest leaves protection of invoice and bank data in database or bucket copies unresolved.
15-multitenant-invoicing.notes:
Confirming sitting on the rulings applied in #1439, sent as CSV in conversation. The own list is the one written on 2026-10-03 before the recorded sets were opened, carried forward. Changed and new findings were marked afresh; unchanged findings (same fingerprint and same text) carry the reader's 2026-10-03 mark, each reviewed in this ballot. The round 2 missing threats are now claims, so the missing list is empty. n refers to the row number of this ballot, which numbered both cases together.
Own-list coverage: items 1-4 map to 33/48, 34/49, 35/53 and 39/45; items 6-9 map to 40/52, 42/47, 41/43 and 34/49. Item 11's database portion is in 50 but needs a conditional rewrite. Missing rows record the remaining paths, not generic additions.
Across both cases, duplicate means the same underlying finding across frameworks; retain requirement mappings on the kept row. Agree on needs-* rows means an evidence gap is supported, not that the control is absent or noncompliance is proven. Conditional threats remain conditional. Only mark and note were changed in the ballot.
Row review notes and proposed corrections:
n=12 [asvs V8.4.1 (authorization); agree; changed]: Supported as an unresolved per-request invoice ownership check. Existing application company filters are acknowledged; missing database RLS is not itself a demonstrated failure.
n=13 [asvs V8.2.3 (authorization); agree; changed]: Supported as unresolved field-level permission enforcement. It no longer asserts that every field is unrestricted for every user; the confirmed mass-assignment behavior is separately represented in 50 and 55.
n=14 [asvs V8.1.1 (authorization); agree; changed]: Supported as an incomplete description of role-specific permissions. The rationale correctly preserves the stated tenant membership and query filters.
n=15 [asvs V8.1.2 (authorization); agree; changed]: Supported as missing field-permission information in the supplied description, not proof that no policy exists elsewhere.
n=16 [asvs V15.1.3 (secure-coding-and-architecture); agree; changed]: Supported documentation gap. The revised text acknowledges asynchronous serial rendering and does not declare all operational defenses absent.
n=17 [stride tampering; agree; changed]: Supported conditional queue-integrity threat. Queue-write access and failure to validate the company/invoice relationship are prerequisites; this does not establish ordinary-user queue access or PDF retrieval.
n=18 [stride repudiation; duplicate; changed]: Same as 52. Keep both under the agreed separate-framework scoring. This wording correctly limits the attribution failure to the database record; it no longer rules out all other evidence.
n=19 [stride information-disclosure; duplicate; changed]: Same as 48. Keep both under the agreed separate-framework scoring. The exposed fields now match the source: invoices, company names and bank details.
n=20 [stride information-disclosure; agree; changed]: Supported conditional exposure of a stolen database copy; readability depends on the protection of the copy and access to decryption material. No absent-encryption fact is invented.
n=21 [stride denial-of-service; agree; changed]: Supported cross-tenant backlog threat from unrestricted submissions to serial rendering. Read the delay as conditional on enough accepted work to exceed available processing capacity; permanent total stoppage is not established.
n=22 [stride information-disclosure; agree; new]: Supported conditional disclosure through the asynchronous PDF path. It explicitly requires both an ownership-enforcement failure and retrieval permission; neither a requesting-tenant job label nor successful retrieval is invented.
n=23 [stride information-disclosure; agree; new]: Supported conditional interception threat on the named internal flows. Transport protection remains unknown; this is not a claim that those connections are plaintext.
n=24 [stride tampering; agree; new]: Supported conditional alteration of render-job identifiers in transit. Distinct from 17: an attacker on a network path need not possess the direct queue-write access assumed there.
n=25 [stride information-disclosure; agree; new]: Supported conditional disclosure from a stolen bucket copy, distinct from the live credential compromise in 57. Encryption and key protection remain unknown.
n=48 [asvs V8.2.2 (authorization); agree; unchanged]: The unauthenticated page uses globally sequential invoice identifiers and exposes invoice, company name and bank details.
n=49 [asvs V8.3.1 (authorization); agree; unchanged]: Supported as an unresolved server-side role check. Hidden buttons do not establish server enforcement, but do not prove its absence either.
n=50 [asvs V15.3.3 (secure-coding-and-architecture); duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 55. Keep both under separate-framework scoring; retain V15.3.3 on this ASVS record. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=51 [asvs V6.3.3 (authentication); duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 53. Keep both under separate-framework scoring; retain V6.3.3 on this ASVS record. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=52 [asvs V16.2.1 (security-logging-and-error-handling); agree; unchanged]: The source explicitly attributes impersonated actions only to the customer user. Preserve both the acting support agent and impersonated customer in the audit trail.
n=53 [stride spoofing; agree; unchanged]: Password compromise permits customer account takeover without a second factor. Do not infer absent rate limits or claim all passwords are guessable.
n=54 [stride spoofing; agree; unchanged]: Supported conditional compromise-impact scenario. The attacker must also satisfy or bypass the office-network restriction and one-time-code authentication; possession of an agent password alone is insufficient. This does not establish a defect in the legitimate impersonation feature itself.
n=55 [stride tampering; agree; unchanged]: The edit handler explicitly saves all supplied fields, including financial state and payout details. Keep the mass-assignment finding. Do not assert that viewers can reach the handler unless the unresolved role check also fails.
n=56 [stride information-disclosure; duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 12. Keep both under separate-framework scoring: this is the conditional invoice-number attack associated with that tenant-isolation evidence gap. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
n=57 [stride spoofing; agree; unchanged]: Supported conditional credential-compromise impact: one service credential reads PDFs across companies. Credential theft is a prerequisite, not an established leak; do not infer write permission or public bucket access.
n=58 [stride elevation-of-privilege; duplicate; unchanged]: Same as 49. Keep both under separate-framework scoring: this is the conditional direct-request attack associated with that role-enforcement evidence gap. Duplicate denotes overlap, not a drop instruction.
